variants.context: Build inputs (context, .dockerignore, Dockerfile, base images, dependency locks, build secrets) define what the builder sees; the build produces a content-addressed manifest and layers; the registry stores and identifies the digest; the runtime creates a writable layer, mounts, networks, and controls around the image’s process.
variants.prompt: A service ships through Docker. Put the delivery path in order.

items.text: Define build inputs: context, .dockerignore, Dockerfile, base image references, dependency locks, build secrets.
Execute instructions with cache reuse to produce a manifest plus content-addressed layers.
Push the manifest and missing blobs; sign, scan, and promote the digest CI tested.
Pull the image, create a writable layer, attach mounts and networks, apply controls, start the process.

variants.hint: Build once, identify the exact artifact, then run replaceable instances.
variants.explanation: Inputs → build → registry → run. The same digest crosses environments; run-time inputs decide how each instance behaves.

variants.prompt: CI must guarantee production runs what was tested. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Narrow the build context and pin base images and locks.
Build and record the resulting digest.
Push, then sign and scan that digest, not a tag.
Deploy by digest with declared mounts, limits, and user.

variants.hint: A tag can move; a digest cannot.
variants.explanation: Deploy by immutable digest when the exact artifact matters.

variants.prompt: A hotfix is being shipped. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Change the source and keep everything else in the build inputs stable.
Rebuild; only the changed instruction and later ones rerun.
Push the new digest and promote it after scanning.
Replace containers from the new digest; keep data in volumes.

variants.hint: Replacing the container is the deployment, not editing inside it.
variants.explanation: Test runtime policy by replacing the container, not by restarting the process inside it.

variants.title: Separate artifact from process
variants.context: The image is a versioned delivery artifact; the container is a replaceable process. Anything that must survive replacement belongs outside the writable layer. Deploy by digest; a tag is only a reference. Containers share the host kernel.
variants.prompt: A database writes its authoritative files into the container’s writable layer. What happens when the container is replaced?
options: The data is lost; authoritative files belong in a named volume with backup and restore policy.
optionFeedback: The writable layer disappears with the container.
Only the image layers persist.
There is no automatic migration.
variants.explanation: Anything that must survive replacement belongs outside the writable layer.

variants.title: Separate artifact from process
variants.context: The image is a versioned delivery artifact; the container is a replaceable process. Anything that must survive replacement belongs outside the writable layer. Deploy by digest; a tag is only a reference. Containers share the host kernel.
variants.prompt: Production deploys myapp:latest. Why is that risky?
options: A tag is a mutable reference; deploy the digest that CI actually tested.
optionFeedback: The tag can point at a different image tomorrow.
Speed is unrelated.
latest is merely a convention.
variants.explanation: An image is content-addressed; a tag is only a reference.

variants.title: Separate artifact from process
variants.context: The image is a versioned delivery artifact; the container is a replaceable process. Anything that must survive replacement belongs outside the writable layer. Deploy by digest; a tag is only a reference. Containers share the host kernel.
options: No. Containers share the host kernel; a VM has its own guest kernel.
optionFeedback: Kernel compatibility and host hardening stay part of the security model.
The boundary is different.
The kernel is shared.
variants.explanation: Choose the boundary from the threat model, not from image size.

variants.title: Order the build
variants.context: Docker reruns a changed instruction and everything after it. Put expensive, stable work before frequently changing source, keep the context narrow with .dockerignore, and use BuildKit secret mounts instead of ARG, ENV, or COPY for credentials.
variants.prompt: Every code change reinstalls all dependencies. What should change in the Dockerfile?
options: Copy the dependency manifests and install before copying source.
optionFeedback: Stable inputs before frequently changing ones keeps the install cached.
Capacity does not fix invalidation.
Cache is the fix, not the problem.
variants.explanation: Read the Dockerfile as a cache graph.

variants.title: Order the build
variants.context: Docker reruns a changed instruction and everything after it. Put expensive, stable work before frequently changing source, keep the context narrow with .dockerignore, and use BuildKit secret mounts instead of ARG, ENV, or COPY for credentials.
variants.prompt: The build context is the whole repository, including gigabytes of test data. What helps?
options: A .dockerignore that keeps generated output, local dependencies, and irrelevant files out of the context.
optionFeedback: A narrow context uploads less and invalidates less.
Base image is unrelated to context size.
Stages do not shrink the context.
variants.hint: What does the builder have to observe?

variants.title: Order the build
variants.context: Docker reruns a changed instruction and everything after it. Put expensive, stable work before frequently changing source, keep the context narrow with .dockerignore, and use BuildKit secret mounts instead of ARG, ENV, or COPY for credentials.
variants.prompt: A registry token is passed with ARG during the build. Where can it end up?
options: In image metadata, a layer, the cache, or build logs; use a BuildKit secret mount instead.
optionFeedback: Secret and SSH mounts expose credentials only to the instruction that needs them.
ARG values can persist in history.
It can leak into several places.
variants.explanation: Keep credentials out of image history.

variants.title: Count the rebuild
variants.context: Docker reruns a changed instruction and everything after it. Put expensive, stable work before frequently changing source, keep the context narrow with .dockerignore, and use BuildKit secret mounts instead of ARG, ENV, or COPY for credentials.
variants.prompt: A Dockerfile has six instructions. Instruction 3 changes. How many instructions must rerun?
variants.hint: The changed instruction and everything after it.
variants.explanation: Instructions 3, 4, 5, and 6 rerun; 1 and 2 stay cached.

mistakes.feedback: Dependent instructions after the change also rerun.

variants.prompt: Same six instructions. Only instruction 5 changes. How many rerun?
variants.hint: From the changed instruction to the end.
variants.explanation: Instructions 5 and 6 rerun; the first four are cached.

variants.title: Place the write
variants.context: Writable layer: temporary process-local changes. Named volume: persistent data with an independent lifecycle, not a backup. Bind mount: a host path exposed directly. Declare state, reachability, resources, and privilege at run time.
variants.prompt: Temporary scratch files that may disappear with the container. Where do they belong?
optionFeedback: Process-local, disposable changes fit the writable layer.
Volumes are for data with an independent lifecycle.
Bind mounts expose host paths.

variants.title: Place the write
variants.context: Writable layer: temporary process-local changes. Named volume: persistent data with an independent lifecycle, not a backup. Bind mount: a host path exposed directly. Declare state, reachability, resources, and privilege at run time.
variants.prompt: Persistent application data must outlive containers. Which placement, and what does it not provide?
options: A named volume; it survives replacement but is not a backup.
optionFeedback: Define ownership, backup, restore, migration, and deletion policy separately.
The writable layer dies with the container.
tmpfs is memory-backed and temporary.
variants.hint: Does surviving replacement equal being backed up?
variants.explanation: A volume survives replacement; it does not automatically provide a backup.

variants.title: Place the write
variants.context: Writable layer: temporary process-local changes. Named volume: persistent data with an independent lifecycle, not a backup. Bind mount: a host path exposed directly. Declare state, reachability, resources, and privilege at run time.
variants.prompt: A container runs as root with the host Docker socket mounted. What is the risk?
options: It effectively has host-level privilege; declare privilege deliberately and minimally.
None; it is inside a container.
optionFeedback: Runtime capabilities should be declared deliberately.
Containers share the kernel; the socket grants control of the daemon.
Performance is not the issue.
variants.explanation: Declare state, reachability, resources, and privilege explicitly.
